changes.before: In agentic robotics, non-expert teaching does not disappear. It moves to a higher level, as people correct plans, evaluate outcomes, and demonstrate the steps that an agent gets wrong.

changes.before: Human teaching would then provide a trajectory at a different level, including not only the motion of the robot, but also the execution trajectory of the agent, that is, the sequence of plans, tool calls, outcomes, and human corrections recorded while a task is carried out.
changes.after: Humans now provide a trajectory at a different level, including not only the motion of the robot, but also the execution trajectory of the agent, that is, the sequence of plans, tool calls, outcomes, and human corrections recorded while a task is carried out.

changes.before: This chapter completes the first stage of this dissertation by turning from human feedback to the other form of human teaching studied here, demonstrations.
changes.after: This chapter completes the first stage of this dissertation.

changes.before: It analyzes demonstrations of a long-horizon manipulation task provided by 40 non-experts in a public space study, and identifies four types of frequent, systematic non-optimal behaviors, termed \thingname{}, namely \textit{Exploration}, \textit{Mistake}, \textit{Alignment}, and \textit{Pause}.
changes.after: The main contributions of this chapter are characterizing and categorizing non-optimal behaviors in human demonstrations.

edits.note: The summary paragraph that opened the chapter was replaced by the stage sentence, the contribution statement, and the introduction text of the paper, which now follows them.

edits.dated: between the commit of October 14, 2026 (3de2b82) and October 15, 2026

changes.before: It presents an online study in which 90 crowdworkers gave either binary or scalar feedback on two identical sessions of a robot performing a button-pressing task, and quantifies how consistent each type of feedback is within and between teachers.
changes.after: Evaluative feedback is natural for non-experts to provide, and can take the form of either \emph{binary} feedback, in which feedback can only be either ``good'' or ``bad'', or \emph{scalar} feedback, which takes a value from a scale of values (e.g., ``1-10'', ``A-F'', or ``0-5 stars''). In theory, both of these types of feedback can contain useful information.

changes.before: Rather than reducing the variability of scalar feedback by reducing its information, this chapter measures how inconsistent scalar feedback actually is, and examines whether its inconsistency can be mitigated algorithmically.
changes.after: This chapter measures how inconsistent scalar feedback actually is, and examines whether its inconsistency can be mitigated algorithmically.

edits.note: The summary sentences after the stage sentence were removed, and the paper's first sentences about interactive reinforcement learning moved up. Hang also made the change of TC-501 in the review of this chapter by hand, with This chapter kept as the subject.

changes.before: This chapter presents the final stage of this dissertation, which leverages imperfect non-expert teaching for learning.
changes.after: This chapter presents the final stage of this dissertation, which is to to learn robust reward functions by combining human demonstrations and feedback, while reducing human engagement.

changes.before: It proposes \textit{Progress}-Heuristicized Inverse Reinforcement Learning (PHIRL), a data-efficient framework that alternates between learning a reward function from demonstrations and aligning the learned reward function with \textit{progress} annotations on a subset of those demonstrations.
changes.after: Thus, this chapter proposes \textit{Progress}-Heuristicized Inverse Reinforcement Learning (PHIRL), a data-efficient framework that alternates between learning a reward function from demonstrations and aligning the learned reward function with \textit{progress} annotations on a subset of those demonstrations.
